name: Diobsud Creek Glacier

itinerary.cal: Best climbed July–September once the unmaintained Bacon Creek Road approach and the Diobsud Creek Glacier are snow-covered/consolidated; the brushy old-roadbed and gully approach make this a seldom-visited, remote objective best done on a dry-weather window.

days.note: From the Bacon Creek Road trailhead (~800 ft), follow the old, downed-tree-choked roadbed for about 2.5 miles, then climb open forest that steepens and brushes up around 2,000 ft. Continue up the southeast ridge past Peak 4800 (the route's crux scrambling) to a camp on the shoulder of the Diobsud Creek Glacier.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach the ~6,250-6,300 ft saddle camp on the Diobsud Creek Glacier, north of Canadian Bacon

days.note: Many parties walk up the east slope at sunrise for a Picket Range view before breakfast, then rope up and cross the Diobsud Creek Glacier, angling northwest and probing for crevasses (often filled-in enough that some parties solo it in firm conditions). The final approach to the modest summit comes from the southwest; most groups linger roughly an hour on top before reversing the glacier back to camp.
days.title: Summit day via Diobsud Creek Glacier

schedule.label: Optional ridge walk for Picket Range views
schedule.detail: Then back to camp for breakfast.

schedule.label: Rope up, leave high camp
schedule.detail: Cross the Diobsud Creek Glacier heading northwest, probing for crevasses.

schedule.label: Gain the south ridge
schedule.detail: Ascend wide-open snow/glacier slopes toward the summit block.

schedule.label: Summit Bacon Peak (7,070 ft)
schedule.detail: Approach the top from the southwest; most parties spend about an hour here.

schedule.label: Back at high camp
schedule.detail: Reverse the glacier and gully to camp for the night.

days.objective: Climb Bacon Peak (7,070 ft) and return to high camp

days.note: Retrace the route back through Peak 4800's crux terrain and down the southeast ridge, then follow the brushy old roadbed (with some shortcut variations near the first road bend) back to the car.
days.title: Descend to trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A remote 2-night/3-day trip planned from the Bacon Creek Road trailhead (~800 ft) on the south side, not the Watson Lakes trailhead used in the approach: about 16 miles round trip with roughly 6,300 ft of gain to the 7,070 ft summit, with almost all the elevation gained on the first day's approach and only a short push to the top on summit day.

approach: Drive Baker Lake Road (FR-11) to FR-1106, then FR-1107 to its end at the Watson Lakes Trailhead (~4,360 ft, Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness boundary nearby). Start on the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail (Trail #611), which climbs gently through forest for about 1 mile to a junction with the Anderson Butte Trail (#611.1); stay left/straight on #611. Continue roughly another mile, rolling over a ~4,900 ft high point, to a second junction at ~4,700 ft — the right fork drops 0.5 mile to Lower Anderson Lake, while the climber's route bears left and climbs about 0.5 mile to a ridge saddle (~1.4-1.5 miles and ~600 ft above the trailhead) where the trail crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness before dropping toward the Watson Lakes. From this saddle, leave the maintained tread and pick up a boot path heading south along the ridge, staying high above Lower Anderson Lake, through meadows to Upper Anderson Lake (~5,100-5,300 ft) — the last easy, reliable water before things get rougher. From Upper Anderson Lake, angle northeast up a short wooded gully, then continue across open rock slabs, scree, and lingering snowfields on Mt. Watson's north side, crossing another saddle near 5,300 ft before descending through heather to the Diobsud Lakes basin (figure roughly 5-6 hours car-to-lakes for a fit party) — the last dependable camp/water source below the peak. From Diobsud Lakes the route turns unpleasant: sidehilling across slippery vegetation, brush and cedar thickets, mossy slab scrambling, and steep dirt/scree gullies with real loose-rock hazard lead up onto Bacon's south ridge. Once on the south ridge, broad snow slopes lead onto the toe of the Diobsud Creek Glacier. Rope up here — the glacier holds real crevasse hazard (parties report needing to probe, especially early and late season, though the upper apron is sometimes reported clean in a good snow year) — and climb/traverse northwest toward the col below the summit pyramid (roughly 6,200-6,300 ft), finishing on broad summit snow slopes to a short summit arête. Snow condition (firm morning snow vs. slushy afternoon) matters a lot on both the gully and glacier sections, so an early start is standard. The gully leading from Diobsud Lakes basin up to the south ridge/glacier access can be avalanche-prone in snow-covered conditions.

approach_variants.name: Anderson Lakes and the saddle chain to the northeast camp
approach_variants.notes: Take the Watson Lakes Trail from the road end and, at the saddle about 1.4 miles in, leave the maintained tread for a hiker's path running south along the ridge high above Lower Anderson Lake. The path opens into meadows and reaches Upper Anderson Lake — the last easy water. Leave the lake heading northeast up a short wooded gully and continue that way onto open moraine and heather slopes near 5,300 ft. Traverse under the Watson peaks and drop to about 5,000 ft to get around a buttress on their east side, then climb to a saddle at 5,360 ft and cross to the south side of the ridge. Continue east, losing a little height toward the next low point in the ridge, a saddle near 4,900 ft, crossing a short buttress on easy ledges on the way. A good camp sits at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of Bacon Peak.
hazards: No tread, no signage and no marked line above Upper Anderson Lake
Lingering snowfields on the traverse beneath the Watson peaks
Crevasse hazard on the icecap if the line drifts onto it
Featureless snow slopes near the top — navigation in whiteout is the real difficulty
approach_variants.baseFinding: The saddle sequence is the proof, and the heights go down before they go up. From the open moraine and heather at about 5,300 ft this line loses height twice: first to roughly 5,000 ft to get round the buttress east of the Watson peaks, then again beyond the 5,360 ft saddle, dropping toward a 4,900 ft saddle reached over a short buttress on easy ledges. A party that keeps gaining height through this stretch has stayed on the wrong side of the ridge — at the 5,360 ft saddle you cross to the south side, and remaining on the north side is the mistake. The camp lies at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of the summit, and from it the peak is gained by climbing southeast. The last test is what is under your feet: this line reaches the summit without crossing a glacier at all, so if the ground ahead is crevassed ice rather than a snow-covered slope, you have drifted onto the icecap and should rope up or come back to the walking line.

waypoints.name: Watson Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: This is the Anderson and Watson Lakes trailhead, the start of the long cross-country line past the Watson Lakes and Diobsud Lakes to the Diobsud Creek Glacier.
waypoints.directions: From SR-20 near milepost 82, turn north on Baker Lake Road (FS Road 11) and drive about 14 mi to the Baker Dam turnoff. Cross the dam on FS Road 1106, turn left on FS Road 1107 and follow it 8 to 9 mi to a signed spur on the left, which ends at the Anderson and Watson Lakes Trailhead in about 1 mi. The road is long and rough; high clearance helps. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

waypoints.name: Wilderness-boundary saddle
waypoints.note: Trail forks here — right drops 0.5mi to Lower Anderson Lake, left climbs into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness toward Watson Lakes.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 through forest to the Anderson Butte Trail junction and stay left. Continue to the next junction, where the right fork drops to Lower Anderson Lake; bear left and climb to the saddle where the trail enters the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness.

waypoints.name: Watson Lakes
waypoints.note: Last reliable water and the only legal campsites before the cross-country push into Diobsud basin; designated sites only, campfires prohibited.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the trail as it drops from the saddle to the Watson Lakes.

waypoints.name: Diobsud basin
waypoints.note: Off-trail descent from the Watson/Diobsud divide into the Diobsud Creek drainage; drop straight to the valley floor rather than contouring from the lakes, which is slower.

waypoints.name: Access gully to Diobsud Creek Glacier
waypoints.note: Loose rock and slick dirt in the chute leading to the glacier's toe once snow has melted out — expect to claw up steep, loose dirt gullies here.
waypoints.directions: From the basin, sidehill across slippery vegetation, brush and cedar thickets, then climb mossy slabs toward the steep, loose dirt-and-scree gullies that lead up to Bacon's south ridge.

waypoints.name: Diobsud Creek Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rope up here — crevasses open on the icecap by mid-to-late season; probe and stay roped through to the saddle below the summit block.
waypoints.directions: Climb the steep, loose gully onto Bacon's south ridge, where broad snow slopes lead onto the toe of the Diobsud Creek Glacier. Rope up here. When snow-filled the gully is avalanche terrain, and it goes far more easily on firm morning snow.

waypoints.name: Bacon Peak
waypoints.directions: Stay roped and probe across the glacier toward the summit block, then follow the flat, often windy summit ridge over a short snow arete and scramble the dry rocks to the summit.
